label: minimal dialect
citation: Steele, G. L., Jr. & Gabriel, R. P. (1993). The Evolution of Lisp. HOPL-II, ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3).
quote: The initial report on Scheme [Sussman, 1975b] describes a very spare language, with a minimum of primitive constructs, one per concept.
note: Steele co-designed Scheme; the URL is a course mirror of the paper (dreamsongs.com copy is robots-blocked). R7RS (standards.scheme.org/official/r7rs.pdf) also says: 'Scheme is a statically scoped and properly tail recursive dialect of the Lisp programming language invented by Guy Lewis Steele Jr. and Gerald Jay Sussman.'

label: a Lisp, again
citation: Hickey, R. (2020). A History of Clojure. Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 4(HOPL), 1-46.
quote: Clojure is a dialect of Lisp, but is not a direct descendant of any prior Lisp.
note: Quote is from the paper's abstract (confirmed via the HOPL IV page and Crossref record for doi:10.1145/3386321; the full PDF returned 403). Clojure is a new Lisp, not a descendant of an existing one.

label: hosted on the JVM
citation: Hickey, R. (2020). A History of Clojure. Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 4(HOPL), 1-46.
quote: Clojure is intentionally hosted, in that it compiles to and runs on the runtime of another language, such as the JVM.
note: Also clojure.org/about/rationale: 'Clojure is the language, JVM the platform.' The influence is the Java platform/runtime rather than Java-the-language's design.

label: functional core
citation: MacQueen, D., Harper, R. & Reppy, J. (2020). The History of Standard ML. Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 4(HOPL), Article 86.
quote: Lisp was the language in which the Stanford LCF system was implemented and also served as its "meta-language." / LCF/ML was implemented by translation into Stanford Lisp code.
note: The paper credits ISWIM (not Lisp) with ML's basic language framework; Lisp's role was as Stanford LCF's earlier metalanguage, ML's implementation host, and the language all designers knew, and it notes Lisp's dynamic typing as its main drawback.
suggested_label: earlier LCF metalanguage; ML's implementation host

label: GC, live environment
citation: Kay, A. C. (1993). The Early History of Smalltalk. HOPL-II, ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3).
quote: I could hardly believe how beautiful and wonderful the idea of LISP was [McCarthy 1960]. / I had originally made the boast because McCarthy's self-describing LISP interpreter was written in itself.
note: Kay credits Lisp heavily, but the full text (searched end to end) never mentions garbage collection and does not credit Lisp with Smalltalk's live environment; what he credits is Lisp's meta-circular, self-describing interpreter idea.

label: unified the Maclisp line
citation: Steele, G. L., Jr. & Gabriel, R. P. (1993). The Evolution of Lisp. HOPL-II, ACM SIGPLAN Notices 28(3).
quote: Common Lisp originated in an attempt to focus the work of several implementation groups, each of which was constructing successor implementations of MacLisp for different computers.
note: Section 2.10.1; Steele edited Common Lisp: The Language and Gabriel was on the core design group. URL is a course mirror of the paper.

label: macros; multiple dispatch as in CLOS
citation: Bezanson, J., Karpinski, S., Shah, V. B. & Edelman, A. (2012). Julia: A Fast Dynamic Language for Technical Computing. arXiv:1209.5145.
quote: Generic functions have appeared in several object systems in the past, notably CLOS [15] and Dylan [28].
note: The paper goes on to distinguish Julia (generic functions as the primary abstraction, like Cecil/Diesel) and says it avoids some 'overly permissive' CLOS features. The Julia manual's Metaprogramming page (docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/metaprogramming/) says 'The strongest legacy of Lisp in the Julia language is its metaprogramming support.', and the 2012 manifesto wants 'true macros like Lisp'; both credit Lisp in general, not Common Lisp specifically.
suggested_label: Lisp macros; CLOS generic functions as precedent

label: functional core without lists and brackets
citation: Landin, P. J. (1966). The Next 700 Programming Languages. Communications of the ACM 9(3), 157-165.
quote: ISWIM can be looked on as an attempt to deliver LISP from its eponymous commitment to lists, its reputation for hand-to-mouth storage allocation, the hardware dependent flavor of its pedagogy, its heavy bracketing, and its compromises with tradition.
note: Section 6. The PDF is an OCR scan ('IswI~', 'LisP fronI'); the quote fixes only the OCR errors.

label: Lisp without parentheses
citation: Solomon, C., Harvey, B., Kahn, K., Lieberman, H., Miller, M. L., Minsky, M., Papert, A. & Silverman, B. (2020). History of Logo. Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 4(HOPL), Article 79.
quote: Logo is, first of all, a dialect of Lisp. / Lay people have often singled out parentheses as their reason not to program in Lisp. Logo avoids this controversial notation.
note: The paper explains that fixed procedure arity is what lets Logo drop most parentheses, and calls the choice of Lisp the most important aspect of Logo's design. Cynthia Solomon is one of Logo's original designers.

label: symbolic expressions
citation: Wolfram, S. (2013). There Was a Time before Mathematica... Stephen Wolfram Writings.
quote: ones like LISP and APL. At first as I sketched out SMP, my designs looked a lot like what I'd seen in those languages. ... I started just trying to invent everything myself.
note: About SMP, Mathematica's predecessor. Wolfram names LISP as a starting point he then moved away from; I found no designer source saying Mathematica's symbolic expressions come from Lisp S-expressions (Wolfram's 'Fast Introduction for Programmers' page on symbolic expressions does not mention Lisp).

label: closures, lexical scope
citation: Ihaka, R. (1998). R: Past and Future History. Interface '98 (Computing Science and Statistics).
quote: The two fundamental differences result from R's Scheme heritage. / In R we allow functions to access to the variables which were in effect when the function was defined
note: The two differences are lexical scoping and memory management (garbage collection); Ihaka also says R began from 'a small Scheme-like interpreter'. The 1996 Ihaka & Gentleman JCGS paper was not fetched (paywalled).

label: first-class functions
citation: Eich, B. (2008, April 3). Popularity. brendaneich.com.
quote: I'm not proud, but I'm happy that I chose Scheme-ish first-class functions and Self-ish (albeit singular) prototypes as the main ingredients.
note: The same post: 'I was recruited to Netscape with the promise of "doing Scheme" in the browser.'

label: closures, first-class functions
citation: Ierusalimschy, R., de Figueiredo, L. H. & Celes, W. (2007). The Evolution of Lua. HOPL III, ACM.
quote: The influence of Scheme on Lua has gradually increased during Lua's evolution ... especially with the introduction of anonymous functions and full lexical scoping.
note: The paper also cites Scheme's first-class continuations as the motivation for Lua's coroutines ('always a source of inspiration to us').

label: whole-array operations
citation: Becker, R. A. (1994). A Brief History of S. AT&T Bell Laboratories.
quote: From APL we borrowed the concept of the multi-way array (although we did not make it our basic data structure), and the overall consistency of operations.
note: Becker also credits APL for being typeless (no declarations) and for careful handling of boundary cases such as zero-length vectors.

label: whole-array operations
citation: Wolfram, S. (2012, May 14). Answer to 'Have you ever worked with APL or J or the K/Q programming languages...?' (Reddit AMA), Stephen Wolfram Q&A.
quote: APL had some really interesting ideas, some of which have shown up in Mathematica.
note: Wolfram says he studied APL while designing SMP but does not name which ideas carried over; he contrasts APL's symbols with Mathematica's English-word names. His 2013 'There Was a Time before Mathematica' also lists APL among languages his early SMP sketches resembled.

label: Iverson's ASCII successor
citation: Iverson, K. E. (1991). A Personal View of APL. IBM Systems Journal 30(4).
quote: The features of J that distinguish it from most other APL dialects include: / A spelling scheme that uses ASCII characters in one- or two-letter words.
note: Iverson also says work on J began in summer 1989 after he discussed his goals with Arthur Whitney (Roger Hui was the main implementer).

label: terse array language
citation: Cantrill, B. (2009). A Conversation with Arthur Whitney. ACM Queue.
quote: Yes, at Morgan Stanley I did use the APL characters, but on my next iteration, K, which was in '92, I gave up on those characters.
note: Whitney describes the line APL, then his own Morgan Stanley APL (A+), then K. The interview supports APL to K; it does not cover q/kdb+, and 'terse' is a description of K, not something it says was transferred.
suggested_label: Whitney's APL line, ASCII instead of symbols

label: syntax, data structures
citation: Ihaka, R. (1998). R: Past and Future History. Interface '98 (Computing Science and Statistics).
quote: Since we were both very familiar with S, it seemed natural to use an S-like syntax. / we found ourselves adopting more and more features from S.
note: The syntax is stated explicitly. Data structures are not attributed to S by name (Ihaka says only 'more and more features from S'), so the label slightly over-specifies.
suggested_label: S-like syntax, then many S features

label: syntax, end blocks
citation: Bezanson, J., Karpinski, S., Shah, V. B. & Edelman, A. (2012, Feb 14). Why We Created Julia. julialang.org blog.
quote: We want a language that's homoiconic, with true macros like Lisp, but with obvious, familiar mathematical notation like Matlab.
note: The Julia manual (Noteworthy differences) says 'Although MATLAB users may find Julia's syntax familiar, Julia is not a MATLAB clone.' The manual describes 'end'-terminated blocks only in its Python and C/C++ sections and never ties them to MATLAB, so the 'end blocks' part is undocumented.

label: general-purpose ease
citation: Bezanson, J., Karpinski, S., Shah, V. B. & Edelman, A. (2012, Feb 14). Why We Created Julia. julialang.org blog.
quote: We want something as usable for general programming as Python
note: Python is a stated design goal ('as usable as'), not a source of specific borrowed features.

label: statistics
citation: Bezanson, J., Karpinski, S., Shah, V. B. & Edelman, A. (2012, Feb 14). Why We Created Julia. julialang.org blog.
quote: We want something as usable for general programming as Python, as easy for statistics as R
note: R is a stated design goal for ease of statistics, not a source of specific borrowed features.

label: let/where, expression language
citation: MacQueen, D., Harper, R. & Reppy, J. (2020). The History of Standard ML. Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 4(HOPL), Article 86.
quote: The basic framework of the language design was inspired by Peter Landin's ISWIM language from the mid 1960s [1966b], which was, in turn, a sugared syntax for Church's lambda calculus.
note: The same paper describes ISWIM as an applied call-by-value lambda calculus 'with syntactic sugar (e.g., "where" and "let" declaration constructs)', and says ML followed ISWIM in strict evaluation and allowing impure features.

label: via SASL and KRC
citation: Turner, D. A. (2012). Some History of Functional Programming Languages. Invited lecture, Trends in Functional Programming (TFP 2012), St Andrews.
quote: ISWIM inspired PAL (Evans 1968) at MIT / a simple DL based on the applicative subset of PAL / Miranda is essentially SASL plus algebraic types and the polymorphic type discipline of Milner (1978).
note: Turner's chain is ISWIM, then PAL, then SASL, then KRC ('a miniaturised version of SASL', where guards first appeared), then Miranda. He also credits ISWIM directly for having no explicit lambdas and for the offside rule.

label: Hindley-Milner types
citation: Hudak, P., Hughes, J., Peyton Jones, S. & Wadler, P. (2007). A History of Haskell: Being Lazy with Class. HOPL III, ACM.
quote: Milner's polymorphic type system for ML would prove to be particularly influential (Milner, 1978; Damas and Milner, 1982). / incorporated many innovations to the core Hindley-Milner type system, especially type classes
note: The paper also says Miranda already had a Hindley-Milner type system, so this influence also reached Haskell through Miranda. Type classes generalised SML's equality type variables.

label: lazy, pure; open alternative to proprietary Miranda
citation: Hudak, P., Hughes, J., Peyton Jones, S. & Wadler, P. (2007). A History of Haskell: Being Lazy with Class. HOPL III, ACM.
quote: Of all the lazy languages under development, David Turner's Miranda was by far the most mature. / After a brief and cordial interchange, Turner declined. / It should be freely available.
note: The committee asked Turner whether Miranda could be the starting point, and he declined. Miranda's licence required permission before distributing an implementation or a substantially copied language, and a freely available language was one of Haskell's stated goals.

label: ML dialect + objects
citation: OCaml.org (n.d.). About OCaml / history. Official OCaml website.
quote: It was inspired by a long line of research into ML / The modern OCaml emerged in 1996, when Didier Rémy and Jérôme Vouillon implemented a powerful and elegant object system.
note: This is the official site rather than a paper. It traces ML to LCF and Caml to INRIA in 1987. Note that it dates LCF/ML to 1972, while other sources say 1973.

label: OCaml for .NET
citation: Syme, D. (2020). The Early History of F#. Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 4(HOPL), Article 75.
quote: The early conception of F# was simple: to bring the benefits of OCaml to .NET and .NET to OCaml
note: The working name was 'Caml.NET', and the 2002 announcement called F# 'an implementation of the core of the Caml programming language for the .NET Framework'. Syme notes it was never fully compatible with any OCaml version.
